stem.v: A server writes its audit trail to /var/log/billing.log. The team wants nobody, not even root, to overwrite or erase what is already in the file, while the app can keep adding new lines to the end. Which command does this?

options.why: The sticky bit only matters on folders, where it limits who can delete files. Linux ignores it on a regular file.
ACLs only grant read, write and execute. "t" is not an ACL permission, and ACLs cannot make a file append-only.
chattr +a sets the append-only attribute. Existing content cannot be changed or deleted, even by root, but new data can still be added to the end. That is why it suits log files.
setenforce switches SELinux between enforcing (1) and permissive (0). It does not take a file name.

stem.v: An admin gives the group write access to a shared spreadsheet and then adds the existing user maria to that group:

$ sudo chmod g+w budget.xlsx
$ ls -l budget.xlsx
-rw-rw-r-- 1 admin finance 0 2024-03-02 09:15 budget.xlsx
$ sudo usermod -aG finance maria
maria, who is still logged in, still cannot save changes to the file. What fixes this?

options.text: Run sudo source /etc/group to reload maria's groups.
options.why: /etc/group is a data file, not a script, and source is a shell built-in that sudo cannot run. It would not refresh another user's session anyway.

options.text: The file can only be written by root, so maria needs sudo.
options.why: The ls output shows rw- for the finance group, so group members can write. Root is not needed.

options.text: maria needs to log out and log back in.
options.why: Linux reads a user's group list at login. The file already gives the finance group write access, so maria only needs a new login session to pick up her new finance membership.

options.text: maria needs extra permissions on the file that she does not have yet.
options.why: The group already has read and write. No more permissions are needed, only the new group membership taking effect.

stem.v: A developer installed a tool into $HOME/tools/bin and wants to run it by name, without typing the full path, while keeping all the normal commands working. Which line should they run?

options.why: The $ on the left expands to the current folder list, so export receives an invalid variable name and fails.
$PATH expands to the current search list, and :$HOME/tools/bin adds the new folder to the end. The tool runs by name and every old folder still works.
Without the $, the word PATH is used as plain text. PATH becomes "PATH:/home/.../tools/bin", which drops /usr/bin and breaks most commands.
There is no = sign, so this is not an assignment. export rejects the strange word as an invalid name.

stem.v: A few help desk staff who connect remotely need to run some admin commands on a Linux server. What is the best way to handle this request?

options.text: Share the root password with them and set PermitRootLogin yes in sshd_config.
options.why: Sharing root's password and allowing direct root SSH logins is a serious security risk, and nobody can tell who did what.

options.text: Ask which commands they need to run with elevated rights and add sudo rules for just those.
options.why: This follows least privilege: each person gets only the commands they need, through sudo, and every use is logged under their own name.

options.text: Set the SUID bit on every program they ask to use.
options.why: SUID would let every user on the system run those programs as their owner, usually root. That is far too broad and very risky.

options.text: Put them in a group that sudoers allows to run any command, so they can switch to root.
options.why: This hands out full root access when they only need a few commands. It breaks least privilege.

stem.v: An admin wants to run /opt/scripts/cleanup.sh as the user svcbackup. Which command does this?

options.why: sudo needs -u to pick a user. Here sudo tries to run a program called svcbackup.
su - svcbackup starts a login shell as svcbackup, and the extra argument is handed to that shell, which runs the script as svcbackup. (su - svcbackup -c /opt/scripts/cleanup.sh also works.)
sudo -l only lists what you are allowed to run with sudo. It does not run the script.
-c takes the command to run, so this tries to run a command named svcbackup as root. The user name is in the wrong place.

stem.v: A user keeps test scripts in /home/dana/bin and wants to run them by typing only the script name. Which command allows this?

options.why: This is not valid alias syntax, and aliases do not add folders to the command search list.
SHELL names the user's login shell program. Changing it does not affect where commands are searched for.
PATH is the list of folders the shell searches for commands. Adding the scripts folder to the end lets them run by name.
TERM describes the terminal type for screen programs. It has nothing to do with finding commands.

stem.v: A user says the weekly "exportsales" tool doesn't work for them. The admin logs in as the user and sees:

sam@app01:~$ exportsales
exportsales: command not found
sam@app01:~$ ls -l /usr/local/bin
total 4
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 41 Mar 04 08:12 exportsales
sam@app01:~$ echo $PATH
/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/snap/bin
sam@app01:~$ file /usr/local/bin/exportsales
/usr/local/bin/exportsales: POSIX shell script, ASCII text executable
sam@app01:~$ stat -c '%A %U %G' /usr/local/bin/exportsales
-rwxr-xr-x root root
What is the problem and how should it be fixed?

options.text: The script has no execute permission for the user. Add execute permission.
options.why: The mode is rwxr-xr-x, so everyone, including sam, already has execute permission.

options.text: The script is owned by root, so sam cannot run it. Use chown to give it to sam.
options.why: Anyone can run a file that has execute for others, whatever its owner. Ownership is not the problem.

options.text: /usr/local/bin is not in the user's PATH. Add it in the user's .bash_profile.
options.why: The script exists and is executable by everyone, but echo $PATH has no /usr/local/bin, so the shell never looks there and says command not found. Adding that folder to PATH in .bash_profile fixes it for every login.

options.text: The user has the wrong SELinux context for the script. Change the SELinux policy.
options.why: Nothing here shows an SELinux denial. "command not found" means the shell could not find the file at all.

stem.v: An audit finds that several local accounts have kept the same password for over a year. Which command brings an account in line with a rule that passwords must change at least every 90 days?

options.why: passwd -d deletes a user's password, leaving the account with no password. It does not set an age limit.

chage changes password aging, and -M sets the maximum number of days a password may be used. After 90 days the user must pick a new one. (You add the user name at the end, for example chage -M 90 sam.)
loginctl manages login sessions, and -H means run on a remote host. It has nothing to do with password age.
usermod -aG adds a user to groups. 90 is not a group name, and nothing about password age changes.

stem.v: An admin tries to join the wheel group and checks the result:

$ whoami
kofi
$ sudo usermod -aG wheel kofi
$ sudo groups
root
The output does not show wheel. Why?

options.text: The words wheel and kofi are in the wrong order.
options.why: usermod -aG wheel kofi is the correct order: group list first, then the user name.

options.text: groups was run with sudo, so it showed root's groups.
options.why: sudo runs the command as root, so "sudo groups" lists root's groups, not kofi's. Running "groups kofi" or "id kofi" shows the change. kofi needs to log in again for it to apply to his own sessions.

options.text: You are not allowed to run usermod with sudo.
options.why: usermod normally needs root, and sudo is the usual way to run it.

options.text: usermod cannot add users to the wheel group.
options.why: usermod -aG can add a user to any existing group, including wheel.

stem.v: Which command recursively changes every folder in the current user's home directory so that only that user can open, read and write it?

options.why: This hits every user's home folder, not just yours, and 750 still lets the group read and enter.
755 lets everyone read and enter the folders. That is not owner-only access.
This targets files, not folders, across the whole system, and 777 gives everyone full access. It would be a disaster.
~ is your home folder, -type d picks only directories, and chmod 700 gives the owner full access and nobody else any. -exec runs chmod on each folder found.

stem.v: User lena can open /srv/reports/q3, but user omar cannot. The admin collects this:

# id lena
uid=1101(lena) gid=1200(staff) groups=1200(staff),1201(audit)
# id omar
uid=1102(omar) gid=1200(staff) groups=1200(staff),1201(audit)
# ls -ld /srv/reports/q3
drwxrwx---+ 2 root reports 4096 Jun  2 10:20 /srv/reports/q3
# getfacl /srv/reports/q3
# file: srv/reports/q3
# owner: root
# group: reports
user::rwx
user:lena:r-x
group::rwx
mask::rwx
other::---
What most likely explains the difference?

options.text: An ACL entry on the folder gives lena access.
options.why: The + at the end of the ls permissions means the folder has an ACL. getfacl shows user:lena:r-x, a rule just for lena. omar is in the same groups as lena but has no entry of his own, and other is ---, so he is refused.

options.text: An SELinux label is blocking omar.
options.why: Nothing here mentions SELinux. The ACL output already explains why lena gets in and omar does not.

options.text: lena is in a group nested inside the reports group.
options.why: Linux does not support groups inside groups. The id output shows lena and omar in exactly the same groups.

options.text: omar is not a member of the reports group or its subgroups.
options.why: True, omar is not in reports, but neither is lena. That cannot explain why only lena gets in.

stem.v: A staff member will be away for six months. The admin must stop anyone from using the account while keeping all of its files. Which two steps should be taken? (Choose two.)

options.why: This destroys the user's files, which they will need back, and does not stop logins.

options.text: Change the user's login shell to /sbin/nologin.
options.why: /sbin/nologin refuses interactive logins and prints a short message. It blocks shell access even if someone has an SSH key for the account, and it is easy to undo later.

options.text: Make all of the user's files immutable.
options.why: Immutable files cannot be changed, but anyone can still log in to the account.

options.text: Ask the user to log in once a week while they are away.
options.why: Regular logins keep the account active and usable, which is the opposite of securing it.
passwd -l locks the password so nobody can log in with it until passwd -u unlocks it. The files stay untouched.

options.text: Set the home folder's date to the day the user comes back.
options.why: A folder's date has no effect on who can log in.

stem.v: A manager wants a list of the IP addresses of everyone currently logged in to a server. Which command shows this?

options.why: /etc/hosts maps names to addresses for lookups. It knows nothing about who is logged in.
who -l shows login processes, not the remote IP addresses of users.
w lists logged-in users and what they are doing. -i (--ip-addr) shows the IP address each user connected from instead of a host name.
whois looks up domain registration details on the internet. It does not list local sessions.

stem.v: A junior admin, priya, needs full admin rights on an Ubuntu server. Which command grants this?

options.why: This renames entries in the user database and can break the account or the whole system. Never edit /etc/passwd like this.
visudo edits the sudoers file safely, but it does not take a user name like this.
A bare user name is not a valid sudoers rule. It would cause a syntax error, and sudo may refuse to run.
On Ubuntu and Debian, members of the sudo group may run any command with sudo. -aG adds priya to that group without removing her other groups. (On Red Hat systems the group is wheel.)

stem.v: A user runs a script and gets an error. The admin checks:

$ /data/jobs/nightly.sh
bash: /data/jobs/nightly.sh: Permission denied
# ls -l /data/jobs/nightly.sh
-rwxr--r--. 1 ravi ops 640 Feb 11 2024 /data/jobs/nightly.sh
# mount | grep /data
/dev/mapper/vg0-data on /data type xfs (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,seclabel)
The user is ravi, the file's owner. Which command fixes the problem?

options.why: The owner, ravi, already has rwx. Adding group execute does not help while the filesystem blocks all execution.
suid controls whether set-user-ID bits are honored. It does not allow running programs at all.

The mount line shows noexec, which blocks running any program from that filesystem, whatever the file permissions say. Remounting with exec allows it. (To keep it after reboot, change the options in /etc/fstab.)
ravi is the owner, so the "others" bits do not apply to him, and noexec would still block it.

stem.v: User "tester" cannot log in to a workstation. The admin gathers:

This account is currently not available.
# grep tester /etc/passwd
tester:x:1005:1005:QA Tester:/home/tester:/sbin/nologin
# faillock --user tester
tester:
When                Type  Source                Valid
# passwd -S tester
tester PS 2024-01-15 0 99999 7 -1 (Password set, SHA512 crypt.)
# chage -l tester
Password expires                    : never
Account expires                     : never
Which command fixes the login problem?

options.why: passwd -S shows PS, meaning the password is set and not locked, so there is nothing to unlock.
faillock shows no failed attempts for tester, so no lockout needs clearing.
"This account is currently not available" is the message from /sbin/nologin, and /etc/passwd shows that as tester's shell. Giving the account a real shell such as /bin/bash lets the user log in.
chage -M -1 turns off password expiry, but the password never expires here anyway.

stem.v: A script needs DEBUG_MODE set to 1, and every program it starts afterwards must be able to see that value. Which line does this?

options.why: This creates a shell variable only. Programs started later do not see it.
This just copies the variable's current value, which is probably empty, back into itself. It neither sets 1 nor exports anything.
let does arithmetic and sets a normal shell variable. It does not pass the value on to child programs.
export sets the variable and marks it to be passed to every command run from this shell, so child programs see DEBUG_MODE=1.

stem.v: Users of a shared team folder can't edit each other's new files:

[nina@srv shared]$ ls -ld /shared
drwxrwxr-x. 5 root design 56 Apr  9 10:31 /shared
[nina@srv shared]$ ls -l
-rw-rw-r--. 1 tom  tom  0 Apr  9 10:31 draft2.txt
drwxrwxr-x. 2 tom  tom  6 Apr  9 10:31 tomsdir
-rw-rw-r--. 1 nina nina 0 Apr  9 10:33 notes.txt
[nina@srv shared]$ echo "edit" >> draft2.txt
bash: draft2.txt: Permission denied
Every user is in the design group. What is the best long-term fix?

options.text: Set the setgid bit on the shared folder.
options.why: New files get their creator's own group (tom, nina) instead of design. With setgid on the folder (chmod g+s /shared), new files and folders inherit the design group, so everyone in design can work on them.

options.text: Change the group of each new file by hand.
options.why: This works once but has to be repeated for every new file. It does not fix the cause.

options.text: Make all the folder's contents readable and writable by everyone.
options.why: That opens the files to every user on the system, not just the team, and new files would still have the wrong group.

options.text: Set the setuid bit on the shared folder.
options.why: Linux ignores setuid on folders. It does not control which group new files get.

stem.v: An admin needs to add the existing user jordan to the sales group. Which command does this?

options.why: useradd creates new accounts. jordan already exists, so this fails.
groupadd creates a new group and does not take a user name.
usermod changes an existing account. -G names the extra group and -a appends it, so jordan keeps all his other groups.
groupmod changes a group's own settings, like its name or GID. It does not add members.

stem.v: Before rebooting a systemd server, an admin wants to make sure nobody is logged in and working. Which command shows this?

options.why: This starts a per-user service manager. It does not list who is logged in.
loginctl talks to systemd-logind, which tracks every login. list-sessions shows each current session with its user and seat or terminal, so an empty list means nobody is on.
-u needs a unit name, and even then it shows logs, not current sessions.
systemd-user-sessions.service only controls whether logins are allowed. Its status does not list who is logged in.

stem.v: An app needs the variable APP_ENV to be set every time a certain user logs in, even after reboots. Which command does this?

options.why: This lasts only for the current shell session and is gone after logout.
Adding the export line to the user's ~/.bashrc means it runs every time a new Bash shell starts, so the value persists.
This sets a temporary shell variable that is not exported and disappears when the shell closes.
export prints nothing, so nothing is written, and ~/.ssh/profile is not a file the shell reads at login.

stem.v: An admin needs to see the UID, home folder and login shell of the account "payroll". Which command shows all three?

options.why: /etc/shadow holds password hashes and password aging data, not the UID, home folder or shell.
who lists logged-in users. It does not take a user name like this or show account details.
getent reads from the system's account databases, local or LDAP. The passwd line shows name, UID, GID, comment, home folder and login shell.
id shows the UID and groups, but not the home folder or shell.

stem.v: What is the best way to make a Linux service account that no person can log in to interactively?

options.why: An account with no home folder can still log in, starting in /.
With /sbin/nologin as the shell, any login attempt is refused, but services can still run as that account.

options.text: Create it with adduser and give it no password.
options.why: Without a password, other login methods such as SSH keys may still work, and some setups allow empty passwords.
Not having sudo rights limits what it can do, but it can still log in.

stem.v: Why do password policies often block users from changing their password more than once in the same day?

options.text: So users cannot cycle through the password history to get back to their old password.
options.why: Systems remember recent passwords. Without a minimum age (chage -m), a user could change it several times in a row to push the old one out of the history and reuse it.

options.text: To make brute-force attacks take too long to finish.
options.why: Brute-force protection comes from strong passwords and lockouts, not from limiting changes per day.

options.text: To force the use of multifactor authentication.
options.why: A minimum password age has nothing to do with MFA.
Complexity rules control which characters must be used. How often a password changes does not affect that.

stem.v: A developer must be added to the docker group without changing their primary group. Which command does this?

options.why: groupmod changes a group's name or GID. It does not add members.
groupmod has no -G option for adding users.
Lowercase -g changes the primary group, which is exactly what must not happen.
-G adds a supplementary group and -a keeps the existing ones. The primary group stays the same.

stem.v: What is the main reason to make passwords expire after a set time?

options.text: To make people pick stronger, more complex passwords.
options.why: Complexity rules handle strength. An expiry date does not make a password stronger.

options.text: To stop people reusing the same password.
options.why: Password history handles reuse. Expiry alone does not stop it.

options.text: To limit how long a leaked or stolen password can be used.
options.why: If a password is exposed without anyone knowing, a forced change eventually makes it useless to the attacker.

options.text: To push users toward passwordless login.
options.why: Expiry still assumes passwords are in use. It does not move anyone to keys or tokens.

stem.v: As root, an admin tries to save changes to a config file and gets an error:

E212: Cannot open file for writing
# ls -l /etc/hosts
-rw-r--r--. 1 root root 158 Jan 12 09:00 /etc/hosts
# lsattr /etc/hosts
----i----------- /etc/hosts
Which command lets the admin edit the file?

options.why: root already owns the file. Ownership is not the problem.
Permissions do not stop root. The immutable attribute does.
lsattr shows the i (immutable) attribute. An immutable file cannot be changed, even by root, until chattr -i removes the attribute.
The group is already root, and the group has nothing to do with the immutable flag.

stem.v: Members of the "ops" group need root-level access on a server. Which file should be edited, ideally with visudo, to allow this?

options.why: /etc/shadow stores password hashes and aging. It does not grant privileges.
login.defs sets defaults for new accounts, like password aging and UID ranges. It does not grant root access.
/etc/group lists group members, but being in a group gives no root rights unless sudoers says so.
sudoers decides who may run what as root. A line such as %ops ALL=(ALL) ALL gives the ops group full sudo access. Editing it with visudo checks the syntax before saving.

stem.v: Batch jobs on a reporting server keep missing their deadlines. The admin collects:

# uptime
 09:12:03 up 3 days,  4:41,  1 user,  load average: 15.90, 14.80, 13.95
# nproc
8
# vmstat 1 3
r  b   swpd    free   buff  cache  si  so  bi  bo   in   cs  us sy id wa st
16 0  10240 7420112  2048 154220   0   0   0   0 8120 2770  99  1  0  0  0
16 0  10240 7420112  2048 154220   0   0   0   0 8098 2781  99  1  0  0  0
# free -h
              total   used   free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:          7.6Gi  512Mi  7.0Gi    24Mi       150Mi      6.9Gi
Swap:         4.0Gi   10Mi  4.0Gi
What will help the jobs finish faster?

options.why: Swap is almost unused, and vmstat shows si and so at 0, so nothing is being swapped in or out.
vmstat shows bi, bo and wa all at 0. The jobs are not waiting on disk.

options.text: Give the system more CPU resources.
options.why: A load average near 16 on 8 CPUs means jobs are queued for a CPU. vmstat shows 16 runnable tasks (r), 99% user time and 0% idle, so the CPUs are maxed out. More CPU lets more jobs run at once.
free shows 6.9Gi available, so memory is not the bottleneck.

stem.v: An admin must unpack the cpio backup /srv/backup/site.cpio into /var/www/site/ and end up back in the folder they started in. Which command does this?

options.why: unzip only reads zip archives, and -c just prints file contents to the screen.
-c creates an archive. This would overwrite the backup with a new archive of the web folder, destroying it.

pushd moves into the target folder and remembers where you were. cpio -i extracts the archive from standard input, -d creates folders as needed and -v lists each file. popd returns you to where you started.
gzip -c compresses rather than uncompresses, and the file is a cpio archive, not a tar file, so tar cannot read it.

stem.v: After maintenance, an admin cannot mount a logical volume:

# mount /dev/vgapp/logs /srv/logs
mount: /srv/logs: special device /dev/vgapp/logs does not exist.
# lvs
  LV   VG    Attr       LSize
  logs vgapp -wi------- 2.00g
# vgs
  VG    #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize  VFree
  vgapp   1   1   0 wz--n- 5.00g  3.00g
Which command is the usual fix?

options.why: lvscan only lists logical volumes and whether they are active. It does not change anything.
vgimport is only used after vgexport, when moving disks to another system. vgs shows the group is present and not exported.

The volume group and LV still exist, but the LV is not active (no "a" in its Attr), so no device file was created. vgchange -ay activates every LV in the group and creates the device files, so the mount works. (lvchange -ay on just that LV would also work, but vgchange -ay is the usual step after maintenance.)
The device does not exist yet, and making a new filesystem would wipe the data anyway.

stem.v: An admin creates /projects/shared for a team. New files made there should belong to the folder's group so that everyone on the team can work with them. Which command does this?

options.why: Execute on a folder only lets the group enter it. It does not change which group new files get.
This lets the group list the folder's contents. It does not affect new files.
setgid on a folder makes every new file and subfolder inherit the folder's group instead of the creator's own group, so the whole team shares them.
The group can create files, but each file still gets its creator's own group.

stem.v: An admin is building a new logical volume from fresh disks. In what order should the LVM commands run?

options.why: pvcreate must come first. The disks have to be physical volumes before a group can use them.
A logical volume is carved out of a volume group, so lvcreate cannot be first.
vgcreate needs physical volumes, so pvcreate has to run before it.
LVM builds in layers: pvcreate marks disks as physical volumes, vgcreate pools them into a volume group, and lvcreate makes a logical volume from that pool.

stem.v: Users cannot reach an HTTPS site. The admin sees:

# ufw status
Status: active
To                Action   From
--                ------   ----
443/tcp           DENY     Anywhere
443/tcp (v6)      DENY     Anywhere (v6)
# ss -lnt | grep 443
LISTEN 0  511  *:443  *:*
What is the best fix?

options.why: The web server is listening on 443, but ufw has a DENY rule for 443/tcp. Removing just that rule lets HTTPS in while every other firewall rule stays in place.
511 in the ss output is the listen backlog, the size of the waiting-connection queue, not a port.
This would let HTTPS through, but it turns off all firewall protection when only one rule is wrong.
Port 80 is plain HTTP. HTTPS on 443 would still be blocked.

stem.v: Linux workstations join a Windows Active Directory domain through SSSD. Which file holds the domain settings such as the domain name and ID provider?

options.why: smb.conf configures Samba file and printer sharing.
PAM decides which login modules run, and most systems use /etc/pam.d instead of pam.conf. It does not hold the domain details.
krb5.conf sets up Kerberos realms and servers. SSSD uses Kerberos, but its domain section lives in sssd.conf.
/etc/sssd/sssd.conf configures SSSD, which links Linux logins to AD. Its [domain/...] section holds the domain name, ID provider and access rules.

stem.v: Which technology does a Linux server typically use to check users' credentials when it is part of a Windows domain?

options.why: sshd accepts remote logins, but it hands the credential check to other systems.
Active Directory uses Kerberos to prove who users are. The Linux machine gets tickets from the domain controller to confirm identities.
Samba shares files and printers with Windows. Its winbind tool can help join a domain, but the authentication itself is Kerberos.
PAM plugs login methods into programs. It can call Kerberos modules, but it is not the domain authentication technology.

stem.v: A new SAN storage array has been cabled to a server. Which command confirms that the server can see the array's disks?

options.why: lsusb lists USB devices. SAN storage does not connect over USB.
lsipc shows shared memory, message queues and semaphores. It has nothing to do with storage.
lsscsi lists the SCSI devices the system can see. SAN arrays connect through SCSI-based links such as Fibre Channel, iSCSI or SAS, so the new disks show up here.
lshw lists all hardware and might show the disks somewhere in its long output, but lsscsi is the direct check for storage devices.

stem.v: An analyst receives a suspicious email attachment called invoice.pdf and saves it. Before opening it, they want to know what kind of file it really is. Which command should they use?

options.why: df shows free space on the filesystem that holds the file. It says nothing about the file's type.
file reads the first bytes of the file, its signature, and reports what it really is. It ignores the name and extension, so a script disguised as a PDF is exposed.
cat dumps the raw contents to the screen, which is close to opening it, and it does not report a type.
tree draws folder structures. It does not inspect a file's contents.

stem.v: An admin's script needs to count how many entries are in /srv/uploads. They start with ls -1 /srv/uploads | . Which command completes the pipeline?

options.why: less lets you scroll through output. It does not count anything.
ls -1 prints one entry per line, and wc -l counts lines, so the result is the number of entries. (File names containing line breaks would be counted wrong, but that is rare.)
tail -f follows a file as it grows. It does not count lines.
tr changes or deletes characters and needs character sets. It does not count.

stem.v: A desktop server boots to a text console instead of the graphical login screen. Which command makes it start the GUI on every boot?

options.why: There is no standard xwindow.service. Display managers are services like gdm or sddm.
The default target decides what systemd starts at boot. Setting it to graphical.target brings up the display manager and GUI login each time.
This switches to the GUI right now only. The next boot still uses the old default.
Unmasking only allows a service to be started. There is no xwindow.service anyway.

stem.v: Which command shows kernel messages from startup, useful for finding hardware or driver errors during boot?

options.why: dmesg prints the kernel ring buffer, the messages the kernel writes while starting, including hardware detection, driver loading and errors.
dracut builds the initramfs used early in boot. It does not show messages.
lshw lists hardware, not messages or errors.
modinfo shows details about one kernel module, such as its version and parameters.

stem.v: A user starts a long job in the background with:
nohup tar czf /tmp/archive.tgz /srv/data &
Which command brings that job back to the foreground of the current terminal?

options.why: exec replaces the current shell with a new command. It cannot pick up an existing job.
jobs lists background jobs and their numbers, but it does not bring one to the front.
fg moves a background job of this shell to the foreground. nohup only makes it ignore the hangup signal when the terminal closes, so fg still works from the same shell.
renice changes the scheduling priority of a running process, not whether it is in the foreground.

stem.v: Commands on a server are slow. The admin sees:

Output 1:
 14:22:10 up 61 days,  2:04,  3 users,  load average: 6.12, 5.90, 5.75
Output 2:
Linux 6.8.0-45-generic (app02)  09/14/2024  _x86_64_  (2 CPU)
02:22:30 PM  CPU   %usr  %nice  %sys %iowait  %irq  %soft %steal  %idle
02:22:30 PM  all  71.40   0.00 22.10    2.50  0.00   4.00   0.00   0.00
What is the system experiencing?

options.why: 61 days of uptime is normal and does not slow a system down.
%iowait is only 2.5, so the CPUs are not mostly waiting on disk.
Nothing here measures network delay. All the numbers are about CPU.
The load average of about 6 on 2 CPUs means three times more work is waiting than the CPUs can run, and %idle is 0. The CPUs are saturated.

stem.v: Which command lists the current state of every service unit on a systemd server?

options.why: is-enabled checks whether named units start at boot, and --services is not a valid option.
list-sockets shows socket units that start services on demand, not service status.
list-units shows every loaded unit with its load, active and sub state, and --type=service limits the list to services. Add --all to include inactive ones.
is-active needs unit names, and --services is not a valid option.

stem.v: An admin changes a server's netplan network config and wants it to undo itself automatically if the change locks them out. Which command should they use?

options.why: rebind reattaches network devices after a driver change. It has no automatic rollback.
netplan ip shows IP lease information. It does not apply anything.
apply makes the change permanent right away with no safety net.
netplan try applies the new config and waits for you to confirm. If you lose your connection and cannot press Enter, it rolls back to the old config by itself after a short timeout.

stem.v: For a malware investigation, an admin needs an exact block-by-block copy of the whole disk /dev/sdb. Which command does this?

options.why: dd copies raw blocks from the input (if) to the output (of), including deleted data and unused space. bs only sets how much is copied at a time.
tar would only save the device node itself, not the data on the disk.
cpio works with files and file lists. It does not make a block-level image.
/dev/sdb is a device, not a folder, so there is nothing to copy with a wildcard. cp also only copies files.

stem.v: An admin wants /opt/bin/rotate.sh to run every night at 2:45 a.m. Which line should go in the crontab?

options.why: This has only four time fields and 245 is not a valid minute.
Cron fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. 45 2 * * * means minute 45 of hour 2 on every day, which is 2:45 a.m. nightly.
This puts 2 in the month field and 45 in the day-of-week field, which only goes up to 7, so cron rejects it.
Cron does not accept times written as 2:45, and there are only four time fields.

stem.v: The package history shows:

ID | Command line     | Action(s) | Altered
51 | install nginx    | Install   |   6
52 | update -y        | Upgrade   |  31
Which command undoes transaction 51, including the packages it pulled in?

options.why: history rollback 51 would undo everything after 51, including the 31 upgrades, and plain yum rollback is not a command.
erase takes package names, not transaction numbers.
history undo reverses one specific transaction, removing nginx and the dependencies installed with it, and leaves later transactions alone.
This removes nginx itself but may leave the extra packages that transaction 51 added.

stem.v: An admin must delete the folder /srv/old_site and everything inside it. Which command does this?

options.why: ln makes links. It never deletes anything.
rmdir only removes empty folders. It fails because the folder has contents.
cut pulls columns out of text, and -d sets the separator character. It cannot delete a folder.
rm -r deletes a folder recursively: the folder, its files and all subfolders. It is the standard way to remove a non-empty folder.

stem.v: Which command gives a full hardware inventory, including system, BIOS, memory slot and serial number details read from the firmware?

options.why: lscpu only describes the processor.
lsmod lists loaded kernel modules, not hardware.
dmidecode reads the DMI/SMBIOS tables from firmware and lists system make and model, BIOS, CPU sockets, memory slots and serial numbers.
dmesg shows kernel messages. Some mention hardware, but it is not an inventory.

stem.v: A PostgreSQL server keeps throwing errors. The admin sees that swap is almost used up:

total     used     free
Mem:        2047600   301220  1746380
Swap:       2097148  2081004    16144
SwapTotal:  2097148 kB
SwapFree:     16144 kB
Which two changes help keep the database running even if the system runs out of swap? (Choose two.)

options.why: Mode 2 is strict accounting: the kernel refuses memory requests beyond its commit limit up front, instead of promising memory it cannot deliver and later calling the OOM killer on a big process like the database.

options.text: Use disk quotas on the swap space to limit PostgreSQL.
options.why: Disk quotas limit file storage per user. They do not apply to swap.
mount -a mounts filesystems listed in fstab. It does not add memory or change how memory is handed out.

options.text: Run dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=64
options.why: This only creates a blank 64 MB file. Without mkswap and swapon it is never used as swap.
In strict mode the commit limit is swap plus this percentage of RAM. Raising it from the default 50 to 100 lets all of RAM count, so the database can still get memory when swap is gone.
This adds swap, but only if that partition exists and is free. It does not change how the kernel handles running out.

stem.v: An admin wants to watch /var/log/nginx/error.log live and also save everything shown into nginx-errors.txt. Which command does both?

options.why: The output goes only into the file, so nothing appears on screen.
tail -f follows the log as it grows, and tee copies its input both to the screen and to the file.
This appends to the file, but nothing shows on screen.
A pipe must lead to a command. The shell would try to run nginx-errors.txt as a program.

stem.v: An admin wants /tmp/app.conf to point to /etc/myapp/app.conf. The two paths are on different filesystems. Which command works?

options.why: This makes a separate copy. Later changes to the original are not seen.
ln -s makes a symbolic link, a small file that stores the target path. Symbolic links can cross filesystems.
touch updates a time stamp and file reports a type. Neither creates a link.
link makes a hard link, and hard links cannot cross filesystems.

stem.v: While setting up a monitoring agent, an admin must make the user and group "monitor" the owners of /opt/monitor and everything inside it. Which command does this?

options.why: chown sets the owner and group together with user:group, and -R applies the change to the folder and everything under it.
usermod changes user accounts. It does not change file ownership, and a folder path is not a user name.
chmod changes permissions, not ownership, and -c only reports changes.
groupmod renames or renumbers a group. It does not touch files.

stem.v: A database moved from 172.16.4.20 to 172.16.5.20. Which command quickly updates every mention of the old address in /etc/webapp.ini?

options.why: awk has no rep function, and awk prints to the screen instead of changing the file.
sed -i edits the file in place, and s/old/new/g replaces every match on each line. (Strictly, each dot matches any character, but that does no harm here.)
perl needs -p and -e to apply a substitution to each line. Without them it tries to run the text as a script file name.
This only prints the changed text to the screen. The file itself stays the same.

stem.v: Which top-level directory holds read-only, shareable program files, including /usr/share/doc with documentation for installed packages?

options.why: /dev holds device files for hardware like disks and terminals.
/var holds data that changes, such as logs, caches and spools.
/usr holds installed programs, libraries and shared read-only data. Package documentation lives in /usr/share/doc.
/lib holds shared libraries and kernel modules needed by basic programs, not documentation.

stem.v: A restore job finds a file and runs file on it:
backup01: 7-zip archive data, version 0.4
Which command extracts it?

options.why: unzip handles .zip archives, not 7-Zip, and -P sets a password.
--lzip expects lzip compression, and v7 is an old tar format. Neither matches a 7-Zip file.
7za is the 7-Zip command-line tool, and e extracts the files. (x would also keep the folder paths.)
zcat uncompresses gzip data. -S only changes the expected file suffix.

stem.v: An admin wants to add the output of ls to the end of an existing file, inventory.txt, without losing what is already there. Which command does this?

options.why: This tries to read a file named "ls", and a single > overwrites the file instead of adding to it.
echo prints the word ls, and sed -i with no script and no file to edit fails.
>> appends a command's output to the end of the file, keeping its existing lines. If the file does not exist, it is created.
This writes into files named ls and awk. Nothing is added to inventory.txt.

stem.v: A cleanup script /opt/bin/purge.sh must run at 6:00 p.m. every Saturday. Which crontab line does this?

options.why: The minute field is *, so this runs every minute from 6:00 to 6:59 p.m., 60 times.
*/18 in the minute field means every 18 minutes, all day Saturday.
Minute 0 of hour 18 (6:00 p.m.), any day of month, any month, and day of week 6, which is Saturday. It runs once a week.
Day of week only goes from 0 to 7, so 18 is invalid, and the hour * would mean every hour.

stem.v: An admin worries that a disk's partition table might get corrupted and wants to back up the raw sectors that hold it. Which tool should they use?

options.why: The partition table lives in raw sectors at the start of the disk (MBR) or the start and end (GPT). dd copies raw sectors, for example dd if=/dev/sda of=mbr.bak bs=512 count=1. sfdisk -d is another common way.
tar archives files and folders, not raw disk sectors.
gzip compresses data but cannot read a partition table by itself.
cpio archives files from a list. It cannot reach raw sectors.

stem.v: An admin wants the path /srv/manuals to be a shortcut to the folder /usr/share/doc/acme/. Which command does this?

options.why: lsof lists open files. It does not create anything.
link makes hard links, and hard links to folders are not allowed.
rsync copies files. A copy is not a link and does not follow later changes.
ln -s makes a symbolic link. /srv/manuals then points to the folder, and anything opened through it reaches the real folder.

stem.v: A customer says their nightly jobs are slow. The admin checks:

$ uptime
 03:15:44 up 9 days, 11:02,  1 user,  load average: 11.80, 11.20, 10.95
$ nproc
4
What is the most likely cause?

options.why: uptime and nproc say nothing about the network.
Nothing here shows memory use. The numbers point to CPU demand.
A load average near 12 on 4 CPUs means about three times more work is waiting than the CPUs can run, and it has stayed high across 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
Disk space is not shown, and a full disk causes errors rather than a high load average.

stem.v: An admin tries to unmount a filesystem and gets:
umount: /mnt/archive: target is busy.
Which command should they run next to find what is keeping it busy?

options.why: ps does not take a folder path. It cannot filter processes by the files they use.
top -d sets the refresh delay in seconds. A path is not a number.
lsof lists open files and the processes using them. Filtering for the mount point shows which processes hold files there and block the unmount. (fuser -vm /mnt/archive is another way.)
du shows how much space is used, not who is using it.

stem.v: Which command shows the block devices on a system, such as disks and partitions, with their sizes, types and mount points, in a tree?

options.why: df shows free space on mounted filesystems only. Unmounted disks and partitions are missing.
lsblk lists every block device, including disks, partitions and LVM volumes, as a tree with size, type and mount point.
mount lists mounted filesystems, not the disks and partitions underneath.
fdisk edits partition tables. fdisk -l can list partitions, but lsblk is the tool for a quick overview of block devices.

stem.v: An admin wants to find which items in /srv/media take up the most space. Which command should they start with?

options.why: df shows free space for the whole filesystem, not per file.
stat shows details about the folder itself.
du reports how much disk space each file and folder uses, so the biggest ones stand out. du -ah /srv/media | sort -h lists them smallest to largest.
Plain ls only shows names. You would need extra options like ls -lS to sort by size.

stem.v: A database process keeps getting killed over several days. The admin gathers:

[Mon Mar 11 01:10:40 2024] Out of memory: Killed process 4310 (postgres) total-vm:4446352kB, anon-rss:4053140kB
$ grep 'Out of memory' /var/log/messages
Mar 06 02:40:42 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 2195 (postgres) score 72
Mar 08 01:10:42 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 5533 (postgres) score 79
Mar 09 02:35:42 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 4106 (postgres) score 90
Mar 10 01:20:00 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 5496 (postgres) score 130
Mar 11 01:10:40 db01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 4310 (postgres) score 260
$ free -m
        total   used   free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:    15819  10026   5174      92         619       5134
Swap:       0      0      0
$ sar -r 600 3
04:30:01 PM kbmemfree kbmemused %memused
04:40:01 PM   5341104  10912068    67.14
04:50:01 PM   5326768  10926404    67.23
05:00:01 PM   5299032  10953420    67.39
What is a possible cause?

options.text: A backup job is using all the memory.
options.why: Nothing points to a backup. The OOM killer picks postgres every time.

options.text: The process is showing signs of a memory leak.
options.why: The OOM killer stops the same process again and again, its OOM score rises each day, and sar shows memory use creeping up steadily. Memory that keeps growing and is never given back is the sign of a leak.

options.text: The system is using all of its swap.
options.why: free shows swap at 0 total. There is no swap at all, so it cannot be "full".

options.text: Cached memory is reaching the system's limits.
options.why: buff/cache is only 619 MB, and the kernel frees cache on its own when needed.

stem.v: A heavy reindexing task is hogging the CPU and slowing other apps. The task must still finish. What should the admin do?

options.text: Run the other apps in the background with bg.
options.why: Background or foreground does not change how much CPU a process gets.

options.text: Lower the reindexing task's priority with renice.
options.why: renice raises the task's nice value, so the scheduler gives other processes the CPU first. The task still finishes, just more politely.
nohup only keeps a process running after logout. It does not change its priority.

options.text: Use pidstat to add more CPU time.
options.why: pidstat only reports CPU usage per process. It cannot add CPU.

stem.v: A timer that should run a report every night at midnight is not running nightly. The unit file contains:

[Unit]
Description=Nightly report at midnight
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-15 00:00:00
Unit=report.service
RandomizedDelaySec=7200
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
Which two changes fix it? (Choose two.)

options.why: WakeSystem only takes true or false, to wake a suspended machine. It does not set a time.
This is not valid syntax. The shortcut would just be OnCalendar=daily.
*-*-15 means only the 15th of each month. *-*-* 00:00:00 means every day at midnight.
AccuracySec sets how tightly the timer may be batched with others. It does not change the schedule, and the random delay would remain.
Without OnCalendar there is no calendar schedule at all.
This adds a random wait of up to 2 hours before each run, so the report would not start at midnight.

stem.v: Package updates fail with errors about one repository. Which command lists every configured repository and shows whether each is enabled?

options.why: repolist shows configured repositories, and all includes disabled ones, with each one's status.
reposync downloads a full copy of a repository. It is not a status check.
This lists installed packages whose names match "repos".
repo-pkgs runs actions on all packages from one repository. It does not list repositories.

stem.v: Outside senders cannot email a company. A check of the company's DNS server gives:

$ dig @ns1.example.net example.net MX
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
What does this error mean?

options.why: A missing name returns NXDOMAIN. Here no answer came back at all.

options.text: The root name servers are set up wrong.
options.why: dig asked ns1.example.net directly, so root servers were never involved.

options.text: dig failed because of the extra MX at the end.
options.why: MX is a valid record type for dig.

options.text: The DNS server that was queried is not responding.
options.why: "connection timed out; no servers could be reached" means dig sent the question to ns1.example.net and nothing answered, because the server is down, blocked or unreachable.

stem.v: Which kind of event would you expect to find in dmesg output?

options.why: Failed logins go to the auth or secure logs, or the journal, not the kernel buffer.

options.text: A USB device being plugged in
options.why: dmesg shows kernel messages. When a USB device is connected, the kernel detects it, loads drivers and logs it there.
Desktop programs log to their own files or the journal, not the kernel buffer.
Session open and close messages come from PAM and logind, not the kernel.

stem.v: An admin suspects that user carlos is running an unapproved program. Which command shows a live view of only carlos's processes?

options.why: ps does not take a bare user name like this. You would use ps -u carlos.
jobs only lists background jobs of your own shell.
top -u shows a live, updating list of only that user's processes with their CPU and memory use, so anything unexpected stands out.
lsof -p expects a process ID. To list a user's open files you would use lsof -u carlos.

stem.v: An admin needs to capture all traffic to or from 192.168.50.7 on a server. Which command does this?

options.why: addr is not a tcpdump filter keyword.
The host filter matches packets where that address is the source or the destination.
net is for whole networks, like 192.168.50.0/24, not one host.
ip only picks the protocol. It is not followed by an address like this.

stem.v: An admin must stop every process owned by the user guest01. Which loop does this?

options.text:
for p in $(ps -ef | grep guest01 | awk '{print $2}')
do
kill -9 $p
done
options.why: ps -ef lists every process with its owner, grep keeps lines mentioning guest01, and awk '{print $2}' takes the second column, the PID. The loop runs kill -9 on each one. (In real life pkill -u guest01 is simpler.)

options.text:
for p in $(ps | grep guest01)
do
kill $p
done
options.why: Plain ps only shows processes from your own terminal, and the loop would pass whole words of text to kill, not just PIDs.
$user is never set, and -eq compares numbers, not text. The test fails.
killall needs a process name, so it just errors, and the loop never ends.

stem.v: A technician needs to download a vendor's software package from a web server onto a Linux box. Which tool does this?

options.why: telnet opens an unencrypted text session. It is for testing ports or old remote logins, not downloading.
netstat shows connections and listening ports. It cannot download.
wget downloads files over HTTP, HTTPS or FTP and saves them to the current folder.
netcat opens raw TCP or UDP connections. It does not speak HTTP for you, so it is not a practical download tool.

stem.v: After changing an Apache config, an admin must make it reload. Their sudo rights only allow the killall command. Which command loads the new config?

options.why: -9 (SIGKILL) kills Apache immediately and nothing restarts it, so the site goes down.
SIGHUP tells the Apache parent process to reread its configuration and restart its workers, without a full stop.
SIGTERM asks Apache to shut down. It stops instead of reloading.
killall has no --reload option.

stem.v: About one in three visitors cannot reach a company's site. One of the three web servers is down. The DNS zone has:
What explains the symptom?

options.text: The zone is missing AAAA and PTR records.
options.why: IPv6 and reverse records are optional. Their absence would not cause this pattern.

options.text: Some records are not signed with DNSSEC.
options.why: Nothing suggests DNSSEC is in use, and unsigned records do not fail one in three times.

options.text: DNS returns all three addresses in rotating order, and clients usually try the first one.
options.why: This is round-robin DNS. Each answer lists the three addresses in a different order. When the down server's address comes first, which happens about a third of the time, that visitor fails.

options.text: The DNS server is set up as an iterative resolver instead of authoritative.
options.why: It is answering correctly with all three records. The problem is the dead web server.

stem.v: Which directory holds the essential built-in commands that every user needs, such as ls, cp and cat?

options.why: /sys is a virtual filesystem that shows kernel and device information.
/etc holds configuration files, not programs.
/bin holds the essential user commands. On many current systems it is a link to /usr/bin.
/var holds changing data like logs and caches.

stem.v: A network team adds a new DNS server at 10.20.0.53. Which file should be edited so the Linux host sends its name lookups there?

options.why: nsswitch.conf sets the order of lookup sources, like files before dns. It does not hold server addresses.

resolv.conf lists the nameservers the resolver uses, for example nameserver 10.20.0.53. (On systems where NetworkManager or systemd-resolved manages it, make the change there so it is not overwritten.)
This configures the dnsmasq service, a small DNS and DHCP server, not the client's resolver.
This configures the whois tool for domain registration lookups.

stem.v: A security advisory warns about "regreSSHion", a known OpenSSH flaw. Which command applies just the fix for that advisory?

options.why: This only checks whether an update exists. It installs nothing.
This enables a repository that may not exist and is not tied to the advisory.
--advisory limits the upgrade to the packages named in that security advisory, so OpenSSH gets exactly the patched version.
--enable is not a valid dnf option, and install does nothing if OpenSSH is already installed.

stem.v: Why does /usr/bin/passwd have the SUID bit set?

options.text: To mark the file as immutable.
options.why: Immutability is a chattr attribute, not SUID.

options.text: To keep group permissions on /etc/passwd up to date.
options.why: SUID has nothing to do with group permissions on another file.

options.text: To show that an attacker changed the system.
options.why: SUID on passwd is normal. It is set on purpose.

options.text: So normal users can update the /etc/shadow file.
options.why: /etc/shadow is only writable by root. SUID makes passwd run with its owner's rights (root), so ordinary users can change their own password hash.

stem.v: A legacy service is being retired. The admin wants to make sure nobody, and no other unit, can start it again. Which command does this?

options.why: disable only stops it from starting at boot. Anyone can still start it by hand or as a dependency.
kill sends a signal to the running processes. It does not stop future starts.
mask links the unit to /dev/null, so it cannot be started at all, by hand or by another unit, until it is unmasked.
isolate switches to a target and stops everything else. It is not for services.

stem.v: An app cannot reach a partner's API. The admin sees:

# curl https://api.partner.example/status
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: api.partner.example
# dig api.partner.example
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 5521
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;api.partner.example.        IN   A
;; SERVER: 10.99.99.99#53(10.99.99.99) (UDP)
The admin knows the name works from other machines. What should be done?

options.text: Open a secure port in the server's firewall.
options.why: The request never got as far as connecting. It failed at the name lookup.

options.text: Enable internet access on the host.
options.why: The DNS server did answer, so the host can reach a network. The problem is which DNS server it asks.

options.text: Review and fix the DNS client configuration file.
options.why: curl failed at "resolve host", and dig shows the host is asking 10.99.99.99, which says the name does not exist (NXDOMAIN). Since other machines resolve it, the local resolver setup in /etc/resolv.conf points to the wrong server.

options.text: Ask the partner for a new API address.
options.why: The name works elsewhere, so the partner's side is fine.

stem.v: A web app needs its database running before the web server starts. The admin sees:

# cat /usr/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service
[Unit]
Description=nginx web server
After=network.target
# cat /usr/lib/systemd/system/postgresql.service
[Unit]
Description=PostgreSQL database server
After=network.target
What should the admin do so the database starts first?

options.text: Add postgresql.service to Wants= in the nginx unit.
options.why: Wants= only pulls the database in. It does not set which one starts first.

options.text: Add Before=nginx.service to the PostgreSQL unit.
options.why: Before= sets start order: PostgreSQL starts before nginx. (After=postgresql.service in the nginx unit does the same thing from the other side.) Use a drop-in, for example systemctl edit, so updates do not overwrite it.

options.text: Start nginx with the nginx command instead of systemd.
options.why: That bypasses systemd and does nothing about the order.

options.text: Mention postgresql.service somewhere in the nginx config.
options.why: nginx's own config has no say over systemd's start order.

stem.v: A user cannot create files in /home/devin/build. The admin sees:

[root@lab01 ~]# ls -l /home/devin/
drwxr-xr-x. 2 root  devin    6 Oct 19 11:22 build
drwxrwxr-x. 7 devin devin 4096 Sep 28 2023 src
devin is in the devin group. Which two commands fix this? (Choose two.)

options.why: The folder is owned by root with group devin, and drwxr-xr-x gives the group no write. 770 gives owner and group full access and others none.
The owner is root, who already has write. This does not help devin.
Adding devin to the root group is a bad idea, and the folder's group is devin anyway. -G without -a would also remove his other groups.
The group is devin, so adding group write lets devin create files there.
devin is already in the devin group.
This changes root's groups, not the folder's permissions.

stem.v: An admin wants new files to get -rw-r----- and new folders to get drwxr----x by default. Which umask does this?

options.why: 0027 gives files rw-r----- but folders drwxr-x---. Folders would lose the x for others and keep x for the group.
Files start at 666 and folders at 777, and umask removes bits. 666 minus group w and x (3) and others r and w (6) gives rw-r-----. 777 minus the same bits gives rwxr----x.
Folders would get drwxr-----, with no x for others.
8 is not an octal digit, so this is invalid.

stem.v: An admin needs to change the hostname "web-old" to "web-new" inside /etc/myapp/settings.conf. Which command does this?

options.why: This prints changed text to the screen but never edits the file.
cut needs one separator character, and this opens a different file in vi.
This only copies matching lines into a new file.

debug1: Next authentication method: password

options.why: That only controls whether root may log in. The admin is logging in as dev.

options.why: DSA keys are fixed at 1024 bits and are outdated.
-R removes a host from known_hosts. This does not make an RSA key.
-t sets the key type and -b the size. ssh-keygen asks for a passphrase as it makes the key, which protects the private key.
-k is for revocation lists, -l shows a key's fingerprint and -p changes a passphrase. None of them make a new key.

stem.v: An admin has uncommitted changes in a Git repo but needs to pull the latest remote changes first. Which command saves the local changes aside for later?

options.why: merge joins branches. It does not save uncommitted work.
fetch downloads remote changes but does nothing with local edits.
stash saves the uncommitted changes and cleans the working folder. After pulling, git stash pop brings them back.
pull may fail or conflict with the uncommitted changes.

stem.v: In IT infrastructure, what is Ansible mainly used for?

options.why: Ansible can configure database servers, but it is not a database tool.
Ansible sets up and keeps servers in the desired state, installing packages, writing configs and starting services, from playbooks, over SSH and without agents.
Process control is done with tools like systemctl and kill.
Tracking hardware and licenses is a separate category of tool.

stem.v: An admin needs to check whether port 8443 is open on the local server. Which command does this?

options.why: tracepath traces the network path. It does not check ports.
dig does DNS lookups. host:port is not a name.
ip link manages interfaces.
ss lists sockets, -a includes listening ones and -n shows numbers, so grep shows any socket using port 8443. (ss -ltn is a tidier choice.)

stem.v: A script prints file_$num_$name, but the number never shows up. Which change makes $num expand correctly?

options.why: Single quotes stop all expansion, so the text prints exactly as typed.
$( ) runs a command named num. It does not expand the variable.
The shell reads $num_ as one variable called num_, because underscores are allowed in names, and it is empty. Braces mark where the name ends, so ${num} expands correctly.
The single quotes stop $name from expanding.

stem.v: Which protocol is used to monitor network devices like switches and routers?

options.why: SMTP sends email.
DHCP hands out IP addresses.
The Simple Network Management Protocol lets monitoring tools read device stats and receive alerts (traps).
DNS turns names into addresses.

stem.v: New DNS servers were added to the network. Which file on a Linux client lists the DNS servers to use?

options.why: host.conf holds older resolver options, not server addresses.
sysctl.conf holds kernel settings.
nsswitch.conf only sets the order of lookup sources.
resolv.conf holds nameserver lines for the DNS servers to query. Where NetworkManager or systemd-resolved manages it, make the change in those tools.

stem.v: While testing a new web app, an admin gets this from curl -v -k:

* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=portal.corp.example

What do the results show?

options.text: It is a wildcard certificate and is insecure.
options.why: The subject is one host name, not *.something.

options.text: The certificate was not signed by a trusted CA, and the check was skipped on purpose.
options.why: "unable to get local issuer certificate" means the signing CA is not in the trusted store, and "continuing anyway" is the -k (insecure) flag skipping the check.

options.text: It is expired and must be replaced.
options.why: It is valid until 2027.

stem.v: What is PEP 8?

options.why: That is pip.

options.text: The style guide for Python code
options.why: PEP 8 sets out conventions like 4-space indents, naming styles and line length, so Python code is consistent and easy to read.

options.text: A Python variable that holds octal values
options.why: There is no such thing.
Those are covered by venv (PEP 405).

stem.v: An admin updated the DNS zone for corp.example, but app.corp.example still resolves to its old address:

$ cat /etc/bind/db.corp.example
ns1  IN A 10.40.0.251
app  IN A 10.30.0.30
$ nslookup app.corp.example
Server:  127.0.0.53
Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    app.corp.example
Address: 10.30.0.99
Which command gets the updated address?

options.why: This only shows resolver settings and servers.
This looks the name up through systemd-resolved, which would return the same cached old answer.
nslcd handles LDAP user and group lookups, not DNS.

The answer is non-authoritative from the local stub resolver (127.0.0.53), so it comes from a cached copy. Flushing the systemd-resolved cache makes the next lookup ask again. (Make sure the zone's serial was raised and BIND reloaded too.)

stem.v: A DevOps engineer needs to start a brand-new local Git repository. Which command does this?

options.why: git init creates the hidden .git folder in the current folder, turning it into a new repository.
config sets options like user.name.
clone copies an existing remote repository.
add stages files, which needs a repo to exist first.

stem.v: What is the name for gathering system events from many machines into one central place?

options.why: Webhooks send event notices over HTTP to a URL.
Log aggregation collects logs from many systems into one central place for searching and alerts.
Thresholds trigger alerts on metric limits.
Health checks test whether a service responds.

stem.v: What is the role of initrd (or initramfs)?

options.text: It is needed to connect over SSH.
options.why: SSH runs much later, after the full system is up.

options.text: It holds the system's trusted certificates and secret keys.
options.why: Those live in /etc/pki and similar places.

options.text: It is needed to set up a random device.
options.why: Random devices are provided by the kernel.

options.text: It holds the basic modules and drivers needed to start the system.
options.why: It is a small temporary root filesystem loaded with the kernel. It has the drivers, for example for storage, RAID, LVM or encryption, needed to find and mount the real root filesystem.

stem.v: An admin must rename a server to "edge01", and the name must survive reboots. Which command does this?

options.why: -H runs systemctl on a remote host. This does not rename anything.
resolv.conf lists DNS servers. This could break name lookups.
hostnamectl writes the name to /etc/hostname, so it lasts, and applies it right away.
This only changes a shell variable for the current session.

stem.v: An admin troubleshoots a network error:

$ ping updates.example.com
ping: updates.example.com: Name or service not known
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by NetworkManager
$ ip route
default via 10.8.0.1 dev ens192 proto static metric 100
10.8.0.0/22 dev ens192 proto kernel scope link src 10.8.1.20
What causes the error?

options.why: The route shows ens192 with an address, so it is up.
The default route via 10.8.0.1 is there.
resolv.conf has only a comment and no nameserver lines, so names cannot be looked up.
/22 is a valid mask, and the gateway is inside it.

stem.v: How would you sum up what Ansible is?

options.text: A tool for monitoring cloud infrastructure
options.why: That would be something like Nagios or Prometheus.

options.text: A configuration tool with its own Ruby-based declarative language
options.why: That describes Puppet. Chef is also Ruby-based.

options.text: A CI/CD tool that automates with pipelines
options.why: That would be Jenkins or GitLab CI.

options.text: An automation tool that uses playbooks written in YAML
options.why: Ansible runs YAML playbooks against hosts from its inventory, over SSH, with no agent needed.

stem.v: Which best describes PEP 8?

options.text: A list of built-in Python modules
options.why: The standard library is documented separately.
Lists, dicts and tuples are data structures. PEP 8 is a document.

options.text: A set of coding conventions for Python code
options.why: PEP 8 is Python's official style guide, covering layout, naming and other conventions that make code consistent.

options.text: A name for the standard Python libraries
options.why: That is just "the standard library".

stem.v: An admin adds a web service on port 80. Which command lets other systems reach it, and keeps working after the server restarts?

options.why: --add-port needs a number and protocol like 80/tcp, and --complete-reload is a separate action.
Without --permanent the rule only lasts until the next reload or reboot.
--reload cannot be combined with adding a rule like this, and the rule is still not permanent.
--permanent saves the rule in the config, so it is loaded at every boot. Run firewall-cmd --reload once to apply it right now as well.

stem.v: Network throughput on a server is poor. The admin collects:

$ ip link show eth1
3: eth1: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 9000
    inet 10.60.2.15/24 brd 10.60.2.255
$ ping -s 1472 -M do 10.70.4.9
PING 10.70.4.9 1472(1500) bytes of data.
From 10.60.2.15 icmp_seq=1 Frag needed and DF set (mtu = 1400)
What is the cause?

options.why: A duplex mismatch shows up as collisions and errors, not "frag needed".
The interface is up and sending, and the error message is about packet size.

The server uses jumbo frames (MTU 9000), but a 1500-byte packet with "don't fragment" set was refused because the path only allows 1400. Packets that are too big get dropped or broken up, which hurts throughput. The MTU must match along the path.
Nothing points to the hardware itself being too slow.

stem.v: What is JSON?

options.text: A text format for exchanging data between systems
options.why: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) stores data as key-value pairs and lists in plain text. APIs and config files use it widely.

options.text: A platform for creating isolated environments
options.why: That describes container tools like Docker.

options.text: A programming language for building dynamic websites
options.why: JSON is a data format, not a language with logic.

options.text: A technique for simulating whole computers
options.why: That is virtualization.

stem.v: A port scan during hardening shows:

# nmap 198.51.100.40
PORT     STATE SERVICE
23/tcp   open  telnet
80/tcp   open  http
443/tcp  open  https
8080/tcp open  http-proxy
What is the best way to deal with the security issue?

options.text: Close port 80 on the network switch.
options.why: HTTP is not the main risk here, and switches do not close ports like a firewall does.
This hides it, but the unsafe service is still installed and running.

options.text: Disable and remove the Telnet service.
options.why: Telnet sends everything, passwords included, as plain text. Removing it takes away the risk entirely, and SSH should be used instead.
A new password would still cross the network unencrypted over Telnet.

stem.v: An app cannot reach a remote PostgreSQL server. Which command checks that the database port is reachable?

options.why: ss shows local sockets, not whether a remote port can be reached.
nc -v tries a TCP connection to that host and port and reports whether it worked.
dig does DNS lookups, MX is for mail, and host:port is not a valid name.
arp shows MAC addresses on the local network and knows nothing about ports.

stem.v: Users cannot reach an app that runs in containers. How can the admin check which containers are running?

options.why: This lists stored images, not running containers.
start launches a stopped container. It does not check anything.
docker ps lists running containers with their status, ports and names. docker ps -a also shows stopped ones.
run creates and starts a new container.

stem.v: A print server running CUPS on TCP port 631 should accept connections only from the local network 10.12.0.0/24. Which iptables rule does this?

options.why: Incoming traffic uses the INPUT chain, -s matches the source network, -p tcp must come before --dport 631, and -j ACCEPT lets it in. A later rule should drop everyone else.
This matches traffic leaving the server, not incoming connections.
-D deletes a rule, and -d matches the destination, not the clients.
OUTPUT is the wrong chain for incoming connections.

stem.v: How is a user's public key used during SSH key login?

options.text: It is used to hash the password.
options.why: Key login does not involve a password at all.

options.text: It encrypts all traffic between client and server.
options.why: Session encryption uses separate keys agreed at connection time.

options.text: It is simply used instead of a password.
options.why: More happens: the client must prove it holds the matching private key.

options.text: The server checks it against its list of authorized keys, and if it matches, the user may log in.
options.why: The server looks for the key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. If it is there, the client proves it has the matching private key by signing a challenge, and login is allowed.

stem.v: Which tool securely deletes a file holding secrets by overwriting its data so it cannot be recovered?

options.why: unlink just removes the name. The data stays on disk until overwritten.
dd can overwrite whole disks, but it is not a file-deletion tool.
rm only removes the directory entry, so the data can often be recovered.
shred overwrites a file's data several times, and shred -u then deletes it. (It works on files, not folders, and is less reliable on SSDs and journaling or copy-on-write filesystems.)

stem.v: What keeps a disk encrypted while it is not in use?

options.why: LUKS is the standard Linux disk encryption format. Data on the disk stays encrypted until it is unlocked with a passphrase or key, for example with cryptsetup open.
GPG encrypts individual files and messages, not whole disks.
OpenSSL is a crypto toolkit for TLS and certificates.
Certificates prove identity. They do not encrypt disks.

stem.v: An admin checks a host on the local network:

# ping -c 30 10.9.0.44
--- 10.9.0.44 ping statistics ---
30 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss
# curl -I http://10.9.0.44/status
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
What can the admin conclude?

options.text: The web server must be restarted.
options.why: It is running and answering.

options.text: The host is denying TCP on port 80.
options.why: curl got an HTTP reply on port 80, so TCP works.
curl reached it over IPv4.

options.text: The host is blocking ICMP requests.
options.why: The web server answers over TCP (403 is a real reply), so the host is up and reachable. Ping getting nothing back means ICMP echo is being blocked.

stem.v: A server will not boot because files in /boot are corrupted. After the GRUB menu it shows:

Decompressing Linux... 
crc error
 -- System halted
Which two steps recover it without wiping the existing install? (Choose two.)

options.why: That destroys the existing install, which is the thing to avoid.

options.text: Boot the system from rescue media.
options.why: The kernel itself cannot unpack, so the system cannot boot from its own disk. Rescue media boots a working system that can mount the existing disks.
Only some files are damaged. The disk may be fine.
Swap has nothing to do with the kernel failing to unpack.
From rescue mode, chroot into the system and reinstall the kernel, which rewrites the damaged files in /boot.
Single-user mode still uses the same damaged kernel.

stem.v: An engineer wants to record staged changes as a new snapshot in a local Git repository. Which command does this?

options.why: clone copies an existing repository.
add stages changes but does not record them.
commit saves the staged changes as a new commit with a message.
push sends existing commits to a remote.

stem.v: Which tool helps automate security compliance checks and vulnerability management against standard profiles?

options.why: AIDE detects changes to files. It does not check against compliance profiles.
OpenSCAP scans systems against SCAP security profiles like CIS or STIG, reports what fails and can generate fixes.
SELinux enforces access control. It does not audit compliance.
Nmap scans networks for open ports and services.

stem.v: Users cannot log in through a directory server. The admin scans it:

$ nmap 10.30.5.12
Nmap scan report for dir01 (10.30.5.12)
Not shown: 997 closed ports
PORT     STATE    SERVICE
22/tcp   filtered ssh
111/tcp  open     rpcbind
636/tcp  closed   ldaps
What is the cause of the login problem?

options.why: SSH being filtered has nothing to do with directory logins.

options.text: A firewall is blocking the LDAP server.
options.why: Blocked ports show as filtered. 636 shows closed, meaning the host replied that nothing is listening.

options.text: The LDAP service is not running on the server.
options.why: LDAPS on 636 is closed, and LDAP on 389 is not listed, so it is among the closed ports. Closed means the host is reachable but no program is listening.

options.text: The LDAPS certificate is not trusted.
options.why: Nothing can connect at all, so the certificate is never offered.

stem.v: A web server will not start:

$ pwd
/etc/pki/nginx
$ ls -lR
.:
drwxr-xr-x. 2 root root   6 Jul 10 10:57 private
-rw-r--r--. 1 root root 895 Jul 10 10:56 server.crt
-rw-------. 1 root root 227 Jul 10 10:56 server.key

total 0
$ sudo journalctl -u nginx | tail -2
nginx: [emerg] cannot load certificate key "/etc/pki/nginx/private/server.key": No such file or directory
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test failed
Why won't the service start?

options.text: The private key must be renamed from server.crt to server.key.
options.why: server.crt is the certificate, and server.key already exists.

options.text: The private key is in the wrong place and needs to be moved into private/.
options.why: nginx looks for /etc/pki/nginx/private/server.key, but the key is in /etc/pki/nginx/ and private/ is empty.

options.text: The private key's permissions should be 0755.
options.why: Private keys should be 0600. 0755 would let anyone read it.

options.text: The private key does not match the certificate.
options.why: The error is "No such file", not a mismatch.

stem.v: Users report that an NFS share keeps dropping. The admin sees:

# df -h /share
Filesystem             Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
10.0.0.5:/exports/team  4.0T  3.1T  0.9T  78% /share
$ ip -s link show ens4
2: ens4: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP
